Phase 2: Research Gap and Extension
Is the method ranking in M4 robust to the masking baseline?

Course: DA351 Explainable AI   Team / members / roll numbers: [fill in]

Colour key: yellow = PUBLISHED results from the original paper (not our experiments)   green = results from OUR experiments (this repository)

1. Original paper

Xuhong Li, Mengnan Du, Jiamin Chen, Yekun Chai, Himabindu Lakkaraju, Haoyi Xiong. M4: A Unified XAI Benchmark for Faithfulness Evaluation of Feature Attribution Methods across Metrics, Modalities and Models. NeurIPS 2023, Datasets and Benchmarks Track. (Full PDF submitted separately.)

2. Research gap

M4 scores feature-attribution methods with perturbation metrics (MoRF, LeRF, ABPC) that replace the top-k or bottom-k features by a baseline value. The paper's definition (Eq. 1-3, page 4, below) says only that features are "masked"; the main text does not state the masking value or test other values. In the authors' pipeline, as ported in m4bench/common.py, the value is the constant grey (127,127,127) for images. A model's response to such inputs mixes attribution quality with how the model reacts to unusual inputs, so rankings could depend on this choice. Gap: to our knowledge, nobody has checked whether M4's method rankings survive a change of masking baseline. Related work shows the issue for deletion/insertion metrics in general (Picard et al. 2025, Rong et al. 2022, Hooker et al. 2019, Hsieh et al. 2021, Gomez et al. 2022), but not for M4's benchmark.

3. Published results (original paper)

PUBLISHED, M4 paper, page 4: Equations (1)-(3), the metric definitions

PUBLISHED, M4 paper, page 6: Table 1, ResNet-50

4. Original approach, reproduced (our run, grey baseline)

Our PyTorch port of the M4 pipeline (m4bench/), ResNet-50, the first 500 images of M4's image list, single grey baseline. Published numbers are copied from Table 1, p. 6; the "ours" columns are our measurements.

method MoRF paper (p.6) MoRF ours ABPC paper (p.6) ABPC ours [95% CI]
GradCAM 0.628 0.657 0.424 0.455 [0.434, 0.475]
IG 0.709 0.739 0.377 0.466 [0.443, 0.488]
SG 0.701 0.728 0.369 0.432 [0.410, 0.455]

Observation. Our MoRF and ABPC are somewhat higher than the paper's. The paper's ABPC order is GradCAM > IG > SG, while ours under grey is IG > GradCAM > SG. The IG and GradCAM confidence intervals overlap, so this particular difference is not reliable. We did not investigate the source of the offset (candidates: image subset, weights conversion, implementation details).

5. Proposed improvement

Instead of reporting one ABPC under one baseline, evaluate every saved attribution map under five masking baselines and report (i) 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, (ii) Kendall's tau and the flipped method pairs against the grey ranking, (iii) a multi-baseline ABPC (mean over baselines) and (iv) the Baseline Sensitivity Score, BSS = standard deviation over baselines of the mean ABPC. The attributions are not recomputed: the baseline is the only thing that changes.

M4 (before)Proposed (after)
Masking baselineone fixed grey valuegrey, black, ImageNet-mean colour, Gaussian blur (sigma 11), uniform noise
Uncertaintynone reported95% bootstrap CI over images
Ranking robustnessnot testedKendall tau, flipped pairs, bootstrap reproducibility
Sample sizeone fixed Nsubset-vs-full ranking agreement (MobileNet, 5000 images)

Supporting references. Rong et al. (ICML 2022): pixel-perturbation evaluations give conflicting rankings, and protocols can be made more robust. Picard et al. (arXiv 2025, preprint): the baseline in deletion/insertion systematically favours some attribution methods. Hsieh et al. (ICLR 2021) and Hooker et al. (NeurIPS 2019): removal-based evaluation can be biased by the replacement value / distribution shift.

6. Implementation

  • rescore_baselines.py (new): loads the saved M4 maps (maps_sq.npy), builds the MoRF/LeRF stacks with baseline_image() + perturbation_stacks(), which keep M4's 100-step percentile schedule and class of interest and replace only the fill value, and stores the class-probability curves.
  • analyze_baselines.py (new): bootstrap CIs, Kendall tau, flipped pairs, multi-baseline ABPC, BSS, bootstrap ranking reproducibility, sample-size analysis, figures.
  • The extension only adds these two files. It reuses the existing m4bench/ image loading, model loading and metric helpers (vision_metrics.batched_outputs, resize_map) unchanged.
  • Same conditions: same images, same saved maps, same schedule, fp32 forward passes. Check done during development on 20 images: re-scoring with grey reproduced the stored M4 curves (per-image ABPC correlation 0.9995; mean ABPC 0.5438 vs 0.5429).

8. Interpretation

  • The grey ranking is not stable across baselines. It changes under at least one other baseline in 8 of 8 models (ResNet-50: black, blur, noise; ResNet-101: black, blur, noise; ResNet-152: black, mean, blur; VGG16: black; MobileNet: black, mean, blur, noise; ViT-S: black, mean, blur; ViT-B: black, blur, noise; MAE-ViT-B: black, noise). A complete reversal of the ranking occurs for ResNet-152 under blur; MobileNet under black; MobileNet under noise. For ResNet-50 specifically, M4's order (ig > gradcam > sg) becomes gradcam > sg > ig under black, gradcam > ig > sg under noise and sg > ig > gradcam under blur.
  • IG and SG are the baseline-sensitive methods. Their BSS ranges from 0.029 to 0.090 across models, versus 0.005 to 0.031 for GradCAM and the attention-based methods; the pixel-level methods have the higher BSS in 8 of 8 models (ResNet-50, ResNet-101, ResNet-152, VGG16, MobileNet, ViT-S, ViT-B, MAE-ViT-B). Under black, IG or SG fall below every coarse method in 14 of 16 (model, method) cases, and IG loses on average 0.18 ABPC going from grey to black (range 0.13 to 0.22). Why (scattered pixel-level masks vs smooth masks) is a hypothesis we did not test.
  • Methods that cannot be separated. For ViT-S, ViT-B, MAE-ViT-B, all coarse-method grey-baseline confidence intervals overlap, so their order, and its changes across baselines, are not reliable. Images per model: ViT-S 100, ViT-B 100, MAE-ViT-B 100.
  • Multi-baseline ranking. ResNet-50: ig > gradcam > sg (grey, reproduced in 84% of bootstrap resamples) vs gradcam > ig > sg (100%); ResNet-101: ig > gradcam > sg (grey, reproduced in 62% of bootstrap resamples) vs gradcam > ig > sg (100%); ResNet-152: gradcam > ig > sg (grey, reproduced in 66% of bootstrap resamples) vs gradcam > ig > sg (100%); VGG16: ig > sg > gradcam (grey, reproduced in 100% of bootstrap resamples) vs ig > sg > gradcam (100%); MobileNet: ig > sg > gradcam (grey, reproduced in 74% of bootstrap resamples) vs gradcam > ig > sg (58%); ViT-S: ga > bt_head > bt_token > ig > sg (grey, reproduced in 32% of bootstrap resamples) vs ga > bt_head > bt_token > ig > sg (59%); ViT-B: ig > bt_token > bt_head > sg > ga (grey, reproduced in 38% of bootstrap resamples) vs bt_token > bt_head > ig > ga > sg (18%); MAE-ViT-B: bt_head > bt_token > ga > ig > sg (grey, reproduced in 57% of bootstrap resamples) vs bt_head > bt_token > ga > ig > sg (69%). This means more or less reproducible, not more correct: the result depends on which baselines are averaged. Grey (127) and the ImageNet-mean colour are close in value, yet even this small change alters the ranking in 3 of 8 models (ResNet-152, MobileNet, ViT-S).
  • Sample size: a random 500-image subset reproduces the full 5000-image MobileNet ranking in only 85% of draws, so the 500-image runs carry real uncertainty (hence the confidence intervals). In our own 500-image MobileNet rescoring the grey ranking is ig > sg > gradcam, whereas M4's full 5000-image ranking is gradcam > ig > sg, so even the grey reference for that model is a subset artefact.
  • Text models. The [PAD] ranking changes under [MASK] or [UNK] in 5 of 5 models (DistilBERT: unk; BERT-base: unk; BERT-large: mask, unk; ERNIE-2.0-base: mask, unk; RoBERTa-base: mask, unk). No ranking is completely reversed. ABPC is lower under [MASK] than under [PAD] in 30 of 30 (model, method) cases (mean change +0.130 ABPC for [PAD] minus [MASK], range +0.024 to +0.283) and lower under [UNK] in 28 of 30 (mean +0.065). BSS by method family: IG/SG/LIME 0.056 on average (range 0.017 to 0.120), attention-based 0.059 (range 0.013 to 0.119). Most baseline-sensitive method per model: DistilBERT lime, BERT-base ig, BERT-large bt_token-23, ERNIE-2.0-base lime, RoBERTa-base sg.

Does the improvement address the gap? Yes for the scope tested (8 vision models and 5 text models): it shows how M4-style rankings depend on the masking baseline and quantifies how much, which the single-baseline protocol cannot show. It does not show that any one baseline is the "right" one.

9. Limitations

  • 8 of M4's 9 vision models (ViT-L not run; this also leaves the PScore consensus with 8 instead of 9 models, which may contribute to our lower PScore: 0.59-0.72 vs the paper's 0.81-0.84 on ResNet-50) and small image subsets (500 for the CNNs, 100 for the ViTs). A 5000-image rescoring was attempted but is not reported: for 7 of 8 models the original M4 outputs for images 500+ do not match the current model on the same image paths (cause not identified), so the stored maps cannot be rescored consistently there; MobileNet is consistent. No PScore/SynScore under other baselines.
  • Text: 5 models (DistilBERT 188 documents, BERT-base 188 documents, BERT-large 197 documents, ERNIE-2.0-base 188 documents, RoBERTa-base 189 documents) of the 200 validation documents; documents whose saved Phase 1 attribution map is one token longer than the current tokenization of the text were left out (cause not found), so N differs slightly per model. Only the best GA/BT start layer per model was re-scored; the saved text maps use the squared reduction (M4's IG/SG metric uses the absolute one), and the forward passes used bf16 (ABPC differs from fp32 by at most 0.003 on a 5-document check).
  • SynScore (section 4 and Table 1) uses 500 synthetic validation images, not 2500, and the synthetic models were trained on the 1271 ImageNet-train images available instead of 10000. Three models (MobileNet, ViT-S, ViT-MAE) did not learn the task with the original recipe (validation accuracy 0.50-0.54); they were retrained with more epochs and a lower ViT learning rate (1e-4, 15 epochs) or recalibrated BatchNorm (MobileNet) and reach 0.998-0.999. Training was capped to 16 GB of GPU memory. For GradCAM and SmoothGrad the softmax-probability gradient is exactly zero when the synthetic model is saturated (ResNet-50 logit gap about 230); in that case we use the logit gradient instead (this moved ResNet-50 SynScore: GradCAM 0.072 to 0.820, SG 0.072 to 0.966; the paper reports 1.000 and 0.998). ViT-B SG stays low (0.22), which we did not investigate.
  • The CNN runs use 500 images and the ViT runs 100, so comparisons between architectures are weaker than comparisons within a model.
  • The saved attribution maps use the squared-channel reduction; M4's own metric uses the absolute reduction. Grey re-scoring still reproduced the stored curves closely (see section 6).
  • Our replication differs from the paper's Table 1 numbers (section 4); the cause was not investigated.
  • Cited papers were checked at abstract / search-excerpt level only.
